sources.publisher: South African Department of Water and Sanitation
sources.title: Water and Sanitation releases 2023 full Blue Drop Report
sources.notes: Release summary reports national NRW changing from 37% in 2014 to 47% in 2023. Full report should be retrieved before reproducing detailed definitions or municipal tables.

sources.publisher: South African Government; joint statement by DWS, Gauteng Office of the Premier, City of Johannesburg and Rand Water
sources.title: Water and Sanitation, Gauteng Office of the Premier, City of Johannesburg and Rand Water on water challenges in Johannesburg
sources.notes: Describes the IVRS-to-Rand Water-to-municipal-reservoir-to-customer supply chain, demand near available bulk supply, and a 35% Johannesburg 'water losses' figure attributed to the 2023 No Drop report. The statement does not reproduce the full metric definition.

sources.publisher: The Presidency of the Republic of South Africa
sources.title: Deputy President Paul Mashatile convenes Water Task Team on intervention to stabilise Gauteng water supply
sources.notes: Reports municipal systems, particularly Johannesburg, remaining under pressure and uses the phrase 'water losses averaging 33%'. The precise denominator, utility scope and accounting definition are not supplied in the statement.

sources.publisher: South African Department of Water and Sanitation
sources.title: Water and Sanitation on significant improvement in water storage across the Integrated Vaal River System
sources.notes: Reports IVRS aggregate storage moving from 96.7% in the prior week to 99.7% in the current week. This is an upstream multi-reservoir system indicator, not Johannesburg municipal reservoir level or household continuity.

sources.publisher: SAnews / Government Communication and Information System
sources.title: Gauteng adopts plan to cut high water losses
sources.notes: Reports ministerial remarks: Johannesburg NRW about 49%, including physical losses of 26%; also gives national and sector policy targets. Report does not state the underlying measurement period or reproduce the underlying water-balance worksheet.

sources.title: Johannesburg Water implements urgent interventions to stabilise severely constrained systems
sources.notes: Reports high demand and excessive draw-off limiting reservoir and tower recovery, low pressure, intermittent supply and prolonged outages across named supply systems. It describes network reconfiguration, targeted throttling, leak detection and repairs as interventions; it is not an independently audited outcome evaluation.

sources.title: Water Loss Control
sources.notes: AWWA describes its M36 Water Audits and Loss Control Program and Water Audit Software; its page reports Water Audit Software v6.1 released in 2025 with carbon calculations and carbon balance.

sources.publisher: World Bank / International Water Association NewIBNET
sources.title: Data Pioneers in Water Utilities - Bangkok
sources.notes: Describes 15 utility KPIs including coverage, continuity, 24/7 supply, NRW percentage and litres per connection per hour, metering, water quality, complaints resolved and operation-cost coverage.

sources.publisher: South African Department of Water and Sanitation
sources.title: The Status of Water Losses, Non-Revenue Water & Water Use Efficiency in South African Municipalities (2012/13 to 2022/23)
sources.notes: The final report is dated November 2023 and presents 2022/23 municipal water balances, NRW, water losses, consumption and Infrastructure Leakage Index. It records 88 WSA datasets (61% of 144); among received datasets, confidence was 55% high, 18% medium and 27% low, while missing balances could be calculated/extrapolated/estimated. Category A metros generally reported more consistently, but the report does not give a specific confidence grade in the Johannesburg Table 10 row. City of Johannesburg Table 10 reports SIV 634,461,668 m3/year, revenue water 328,709,771 m3/year, NRW 305,751,897 m3/year, NRW share 48.2%, 280 litres/capita/day and ILI 9.3. Source bytes have not yet been snapshotted.

sources.publisher: South African Department of Water and Sanitation
sources.title: 2023 No Drop Report
sources.notes: Johannesburg scorecard is based on the 2021/22 audit period. The City received an overall No Drop score of 72%: strategy/planning/implementation 91%, asset management 50%, technical skills 80%, compliance/performance 24%, weighted subtotal 62%, plus a 10% bonus. It notes high-integrity IWA water balance, insufficient consumer meter maintenance interventions and no evidence of a leak-repair schedule for the audit period. The No Drop score is an institutional/regulatory assessment, not a water-loss percentage.

sources.title: Johannesburg Water Annual Report 2023/2024
sources.notes: The report's annual performance narrative and Note 27 report FY2023/24 NRW 46.18% (2023: 46.11%), comprising 24.83% physical losses, 9.66% commercial losses and 11.69% unbilled authorised consumption. Combined physical and commercial losses are 34.49% (2023: 33.41%); these are part of NRW, not the same metric as total NRW. The report notes FY2023/24 average asset renewal rate of 1.0% against the 1.5% annual replacement-value reference rate in asset plans, an R32.54bn renewal backlog, 26% of the asset base with under 10 years' remaining life, and operational reservoir/zonal meters increasing from 50% to 60%. Source bytes have not yet been snapshotted.

sources.title: EPANET — Application for Modeling Drinking Water Distribution Systems
sources.notes: EPA describes EPANET as an extended-period hydraulic and water-quality simulator for pressurized networks with pipes, junctions, pumps, valves, tanks and reservoirs. It tracks flow, pressure, tank levels, chemical concentration, water age and source tracing; supports pressure-dependent demands, friction headloss formulas, pump energy and operational controls. Use as an external hydraulic reference where inputs and physical assumptions are aligned. It is not an institutional/governance simulator.

sources.title: OpenFlows Water — Water Distribution Modeling Software
sources.notes: Bentley lists steady-state and extended-period hydraulic simulation, water quality, pressure, flow, pump performance, transient/water-hammer analysis, GIS/CAD/SCADA integration and asset/pipe-renewal planning capabilities. Product feature claims are vendor-published and are a commercial industry comparator, not independent evidence of performance.

sources.publisher: Journal of Water Process Engineering / Elsevier
sources.title: Benchmarking Diverse Learning Architectures for Leak Detection and Localization in Water Distribution Systems
sources.notes: Abstract reports 47,000+ EPANET/WNTR Net3 scenarios, >95% binary detection, and ensemble ML Top-1 localization around 75–77%, with robustness checks across leak size, sensor density and noise. This is a Net3 synthetic task; do not treat as field-transfer evidence or compare its Top-1 directly with distance-threshold localization on another benchmark.

sources.title: Deep learning for leakage detection in water distribution networks: a systematic review and benchmark
sources.notes: Abstract reports review of 244 records / 71 pure-DL studies and an experimental benchmark. Reported abstract metrics include time-transformer detection accuracy 96.1% (AUC 0.94), GGNN localization success 88.5% within 300m, and 1D-CNN autoencoder accuracy 92.6% with 3.5ms inference. The tasks, topology, measurement assumptions and hardware must be checked in the full paper before any like-for-like comparison. The review reports major data/code and inference-time reporting gaps.

sources.title: Explainable simulation-to-field transfer learning for transient-based leak detection in water distribution networks
sources.notes: Abstract reports an expanded 40-scenario experimental test under a different PRV set pressure: transfer learning improved best classification from 30.00% direct-test to 62.50% after transfer, and reduced leak-location MAE from 18.44m to 6.57m. This is a transient sensing modality and a distinct experiment, not directly comparable to Net3 pipe/node classification.

sources.title: Standardization and Benchmarking of Datasets and Evaluation Protocols for Machine Learning-Based Water Leak Detection: A Systematic Review
sources.notes: Review of 90 studies highlights inconsistent dataset generation, splits, metrics and scenario definitions as barriers to fair comparison. It recommends standardized dataset documentation, evaluation protocols, uncertainty quantification, interpretability and expanded shared benchmarks.

relationships.interpretation: 34.49_percent_is_24.83_percent_physical_plus_9.66_percent_commercial_losses; it excludes 11.69_percent unbilled_authorised_consumption and is therefore not the 46.18_percent NRW value
No_Drop_score_assesses_water_conservation_demand_management_capability_and_compliance; it is not a substitute for a physical water-balance metric

the 2024 joint statement's approximately 35_percent water-loss wording is close to the utility's audited FY2023/24 combined physical-plus-commercial loss figure of 34.49_percent; the statement does not state a matching measurement period or denominator, so identity of the two observations is not established

targets.notes: The article phrases this as all schools and clinics; the 100% representation is a normalized interpretation.

comparability_rules: Do not compare percentages unless metric definition, numerator, denominator, system boundary, geography, observation period and data-quality grade are compatible.
Physical water losses are a component of non-revenue water where explicitly defined as such; do not add them to NRW.
The 2023 Johannesburg 35% 'water losses' figure and the February 2026 33% 'water losses' figure remain untyped until their underlying water-balance definitions are retrieved.
The October 2026 49% NRW and 26% physical-loss figures are minister-reported estimates; the underlying audit workbook and measurement period are not included in the news article.
IVRS reservoir storage is an upstream resource-state observation and cannot be used as a proxy for municipal distribution reliability or household service continuity.
Policy targets are not observations or achieved outcomes.
Planned or in-progress interventions are not verified completion or measured impact.
Missing source data is unknown, not zero.

DWS 2022/23 Table 10 reports City of Johannesburg NRW 48.2%, SIV 634,461,668 kL/year, revenue water 328,709,771 kL/year, NRW volume 305,751,897 kL/year, 280 litres/capita/day and ILI 9.3. Preserve the report's year and units.

Johannesburg Water's FY2023/24 audited financial statement reports NRW 46.18%, physical losses 24.83%, commercial losses 9.66% and unbilled authorised consumption 11.69%; the components sum to 46.18% within rounding.

The same Johannesburg Water Note 27 defines combined water losses (physical plus commercial) at 34.49% for FY2023/24 and 33.41% for FY2022/23. These are components of NRW and exclude unbilled authorised consumption; do not label them total NRW.

The Johannesburg 2021/22 No Drop score of 72% is an institutional/regulatory assessment score, not a leakage, NRW or service-continuity percentage. Criterion scores include asset management 50% and compliance/performance 24%.

DWS's 2023 technical benchmarking report and the 2023 No Drop regulatory audit are different products with different reporting periods and scoring purposes; never conflate the No Drop score with the water-balance values.

DWS Table 10 volume values are cubic metres per year (m3/year), not kilolitres per year. The City of Johannesburg 2022/23 SIV of 634,461,668 m3/year is about 1,738 ML/day when converted using 365 days; this derived conversion must retain the source boundary and year.

The 2023 DWS benchmark report's 88 submissions (61% of WSAs) had mixed confidence: 55% high, 18% medium and 27% low among received datasets. Missing WSA balances could be calculated, extrapolated or estimated. Do not assume a per-municipality confidence level unless explicitly supplied.

Johannesburg Water's FY2023/24 report says 34.49% combined physical+commercial losses and 46.18% total NRW; the approximately 35% wording in the November 2024 joint government statement is close to this combined-loss definition, but the two should not be treated as the same observation without period/denominator confirmation.
The No Drop 72% score is not NRW, physical loss, water quality or continuity. It is an institutional WC/WDM assessment for the 2021/22 audit period.

EPANET is an external physical reference model, not an institutional policy evaluator. Compare only like-for-like hydraulic and water-quality outputs under aligned topology, units, demand profiles, controls, boundary conditions and time steps.

OpenFlows feature descriptions are vendor-published product claims. Product presence is not performance evidence; any comparison requires an exact benchmark case, product/version, input model, hardware and measured outputs.
The water core's discrete storage/allocation profiles are not hydraulic simulations and must not be represented as a replacement for EPANET or OpenFlows.

benchmark_alignment.awwa: Use AWWA M36 / Water Audit Software concepts as the water-audit and loss-control baseline; do not claim to replace AWWA.
benchmark_alignment.newibnet: Map utility KPIs to NewIBNET indicators including continuity, 24/7 supply, NRW percent, NRW per connection per hour, metering, water quality and complaints resolved.
benchmark_alignment.civbench_extension: Add typed multi-layer evidence, physical stock-flow, service continuity, quality, equity, maintenance, recovery, institutional dependency, and long-run feedback without collapsing outcomes into one score.
benchmark_alignment.epanet: EPA EPANET 2.2 is the hydraulic/water-quality reference solver for pressurized distribution cases; compose through Sol-Atlas #139, not a parallel hydraulic engine.
benchmark_alignment.openflows: Bentley OpenFlows Water is a commercial engineering-product comparator for hydraulic, water-quality, transient, GIS/SCADA and renewal-planning workflows; do not claim equivalent functionality without an apples-to-apples evaluation.
benchmark_alignment.leak_detection_sota: Keep binary detection, pipe/node localization, distance-threshold localization, held-out topology, operating/data shift, simulation-to-field transfer and value-of-information as separate benchmark lanes. 2026 papers report incompatible metrics and datasets; use their results as protocol-specific reference points, never one blended SOTA number. See Ranganathan Net3, Tarawneh review, Water Research transient field-transfer study, and the 2026 standardization review in sources.
